problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)=\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨3,3⟩,$ respectively.
worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨3,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,3)-f(0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨3,3⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\ \sqrt{25-{3}^{2}}-\sqrt{25-{0}^{2}} & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,3⟩ \\ 4-5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,3⟩ \\ -1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-\frac{x}{\sqrt{25-{x}^{2}}},0⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-\frac{{c}_{1}}{\sqrt{25-{c}_{1}^{2}}},0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,3⟩ \\ -1 & =⟨-\frac{{c}_{1}}{\sqrt{25-{c}_{1}^{2}}},0⟩\cdot ⟨3,3⟩ \\ -1 & =-\frac{3{c}_{1}}{\sqrt{25-{c}_{1}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{25-{c}_{1}^{2}} & =3{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve this radical equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{25-{c}_{1}^{2}} & =3{c}_{1} \\ 25-{c}_{1}^{2} & =9{c}_{1}^{2} \\ 10{c}_{1}^{2} & =25 \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{5}{2} \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting back into the radical equation, we notice that ${c}_{1}=-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}$ does not satisfy the equation. Therefore, the only solution is ${c}_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{2}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-0}{3-0} & =\frac{x-0}{3-0} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =\frac{x}{3} \\ y & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2},$ we obtain that ${c}_{2}={c}_{1}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}).$
